claim: In mouse and human, genes subjected to genomic imprinting have been shown to function in development, behavior, and post-natal adaptations.
source: In mouse and human, genes subjected to genomic imprinting have been shown to function in development, behavior, and post-natal adaptations.
evidence: This is a general statement about the known functions of imprinted genes, drawing from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Failure to correctly imprint genes in human is associated with developmental syndromes, adaptive, and metabolic disorders during life as well as numerous forms of cancer.
source: Failure to correctly imprint genes in human is associated with developmental syndromes, adaptive, and metabolic disorders during life as well as numerous forms of cancer.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction section referencing Ishida and Moore, 2013 and Uribe-Lewis et al., 2011.

claim: In recent years researchers have turned to RNA-seq technologies applied to reciprocal hybrid strains of mice to identify novel imprinted genes, causing a threefold increase in genes reported as having a parental origin-specific expression bias.
source: In recent years researchers have turned to RNA-seq technologies applied to reciprocal hybrid strains of mice to identify novel imprinted genes, causing a threefold increase in genes reported as having a parental origin-specific expression bias.
evidence: This claim is supported by the meta-analysis of multiple RNA-seq studies presented in the manuscript.

claim: The methods used to generate and analyze libraries greatly influence the calling of allele-specific expression.
source: Here, we present an in-depth meta-analysis of previously generated RNA-seq data and show that the methods used to generate and analyze libraries greatly influence the calling of allele-specific expression.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the reanalysis of multiple datasets using the same pipeline, showing different results than the original studies.

claim: Most novel genes called with parental-origin-specific allelic bias are artefactual.
source: Validation experiments show that most novel genes called with parental-origin-specific allelic bias are artefactual, with the mouse strain contributing a larger effect on expression biases than parental origin.
evidence: This is supported by experimental validation via pyrosequencing of 43 genes, showing most do not validate.

claim: The mouse strain contributes a larger effect on expression biases than parental origin for most novel genes.
source: Validation experiments show that most novel genes called with parental-origin-specific allelic bias are artefactual, with the mouse strain contributing a larger effect on expression biases than parental origin.
evidence: This is supported by the observation that more genes showed strain bias than parental bias in the validation experiments.

claim: Most weak novel genes that do validate are located at the periphery of known imprinted domains.
source: Of the weak novel genes that do validate, most are located at the periphery of known imprinted domains, suggesting they may be affected by local allele- and tissue-specific conformation.
evidence: This is supported by the classification of genes into Class-3 (near known imprinted genes) and the validation data showing Class-3 genes are more likely to validate than Class-1 or Class-2 genes.

claim: Weak biased genes at the periphery of imprinted domains may be affected by local allele- and tissue-specific conformation.
source: Of the weak novel genes that do validate, most are located at the periphery of known imprinted domains, suggesting they may be affected by local allele- and tissue-specific conformation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the validation data and the observation that weak biases are found at cluster peripheries.

claim: Approximately 150 imprinted genes have been identified in mice and humans.
source: To date, approximately 150 imprinted genes have been identified in mice and humans where they have been shown to have vital roles in development, behavior, and post-natal adaptations (Tucci et al., 2019; Plasschaert and Bartolomei, 2014; Cleaton et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles summarizing the field.

claim: Germline differentially methylated regions (gDMRs) associated with imprinted genes are protected from the global demethylation that occurs in the zygote.
source: Germline differentially methylated regions (gDMRs) associated with imprinted genes differ from others because they are protected from the global demethylation that occurs in the zygote; a process requiring the KRAB-zinc finger proteins Zfp57 and Zfp445 (Li et al., 2008; Takahashi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on Zfp57 and Zfp445.

claim: Protection of gDMRs from demethylation requires the KRAB-zinc finger proteins Zfp57 and Zfp445.
source: Germline differentially methylated regions (gDMRs) associated with imprinted genes differ from others because they are protected from the global demethylation that occurs in the zygote; a process requiring the KRAB-zinc finger proteins Zfp57 and Zfp445 (Li et al., 2008; Takahashi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li et al., 2008 and Takahashi et al., 2019.

claim: Imprinted genes are frequently organized into clusters or pairs in the genome.
source: Imprinted genes are frequently organized into clusters or pairs in the genome and a single gDMR acts as an imprinting control region (ICR) for the entire domain (Edwards and Ferguson-Smith, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by a citation.

claim: A single gDMR acts as an imprinting control region (ICR) for the entire imprinted domain.
source: Imprinted genes are frequently organized into clusters or pairs in the genome and a single gDMR acts as an imprinting control region (ICR) for the entire domain (Edwards and Ferguson-Smith, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Secondary or somatic DMRs are established after fertilization, under the control of the ICR.
source: Secondary or somatic DMRs are also associated with imprinted genes: these DMRs are established after fertilization, under the control of the ICR, and are generally not bound by Zfp57 and or Zfp445.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the timing and control of somatic DMRs.

claim: Somatic DMRs are generally not bound by Zfp57 and Zfp445.
source: Secondary or somatic DMRs are also associated with imprinted genes: these DMRs are established after fertilization, under the control of the ICR, and are generally not bound by Zfp57 and or Zfp445.
evidence: This is established knowledge distinguishing somatic DMRs from germline DMRs.

claim: Non-canonically imprinted genes show paternally biased expression in the preimplantation embryo which persists in extra-embryonic tissue but is lost in the embryo proper.
source: More recently Inoue et al., identified a germline-derived histone 3 lysine 27 tri-methylation (H3K27me3) mediated mechanism that also can confer parental origin-specific expression. These 'non-canonically' imprinted genes show paternally biased expression in the preimplantation embryo which persists in extra-embryonic tissue but is lost in the embryo proper (Inoue et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Inoue et al., 2017.

claim: In 2010 two related works reported approximately 1300 new imprinted genes in the brain.
source: For example, in 2010 two related works reported approximately 1300 new imprinted genes in the brain, which would have increased the number of known imprinted genes in the mouse by an order of magnitude (Gregg et al., 2010b; Gregg et al., 2010a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gregg et al., 2010a and 2010b.

claim: The 2010 datasets reporting 1300 new imprinted genes were subsequently shown to include multiple false positives.
source: These datasets were subsequently shown to include multiple false positives emphasizing the need for validation of putative imprinted genes via a complementary method (DeVeale et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to DeVeale et al., 2012.

claim: Only 36 out of 313 genes (11.5%) were identified with allelic biases in all four studies analyzed.
source: This produced a list of 313 genes of which only 36 (11.5%) were identified with allelic biases in all four studies (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is a direct result from the meta-analysis comparing the four datasets.

claim: 30 out of 87 (35%) known genes were identified in all four studies.
source: When the overlap between studies was assessed, 30 out of 87 (35%) known genes were identified in all four studies compared with six out of 226 novel genes (2.7%) (Figure 1A and B and Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the overlap analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Only 6 out of 226 (2.7%) novel genes were identified in all four studies.
source: When the overlap between studies was assessed, 30 out of 87 (35%) known genes were identified in all four studies compared with six out of 226 novel genes (2.7%) (Figure 1A and B and Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the overlap analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: The only six novel genes that came up in all four studies belong to Class-3.
source: Indeed, the only six novel genes that came up in all four studies belong to Class-3 (Figure 1C) indicating that the boundaries of some imprinting clusters may not have been fully defined previously.
evidence: This is a result from the overlap analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: 82.7% of novel parental-origin-specific biased genes were unique to one study.
source: The vast majority (82.7%) of novel parental-origin-specific biased genes were unique to one study, whereas only 28.7% of known genes fell in the same category (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the overlap analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Only 28.7% of known genes were unique to one study.
source: The vast majority (82.7%) of novel parental-origin-specific biased genes were unique to one study, whereas only 28.7% of known genes fell in the same category (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the overlap analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: 66% of total known genes and 17% of Class-3 genes overlap between Dataset A calls and ISoLDE calls.
source: 66% of total known genes and 17% of Class-3 genes overlap using their approach and ISoLDE (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a result from the reanalysis of Dataset A using ISoLDE.

claim: ISoLDE identified a high proportion of Class-1+2 genes (65.2%) in Dataset A.
source: For these data, ISoLDE identified a high proportion of Class-1 +2 genes (65.2%).
evidence: This is a result from the reanalysis of Dataset A using ISoLDE.

claim: The high number of novel genes called by ISoLDE in Dataset A is most likely due to the absence of biological replicates.
source: This high number of novel genes called by ISoLDE is most likely due to the absence of biological replicates in Dataset A as other datasets without biological replicates also have increased novel calls (data not shown).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with other datasets.

claim: For Dataset B, 49 known genes overlap which is 73% of all genes identified using both methods.
source: For Dataset B, 49 known genes overlap which is 73% of all genes identified using both methods (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a result from the reanalysis of Dataset B using ISoLDE.

claim: For Dataset C, 67% of known genes overlapped between the original study and ISoLDE analysis.
source: A similar pattern is observed in the Dataset C with 67% of known genes overlapping, 14% of Class-3, and 8% of Class-1 +2 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a result from the reanalysis of Dataset C using ISoLDE.

claim: Nine out of 20 known imprinted genes identified in the two liver datasets overlapped (45%).
source: Nine out of 20 known imprinted genes identified in the two liver datasets overlapped (45% - Figure 2D)
evidence: This is a result from comparing liver data from Datasets A and B using the same pipeline.

claim: 20 of 29 known genes overlapped in muscle datasets (69%).
source: 20 of 29 in muscle (69% - Figure 2E)
evidence: This is a result from comparing muscle data from Datasets A and B using the same pipeline.

claim: 37 of 53 known genes overlapped in the hypothalamus (70%).
source: 37 of 53 in the hypothalamus (70% - Figure 2F)
evidence: This is a result from comparing hypothalamus data from Datasets A and B using the same pipeline.

claim: 24 of 49 known genes overlapped in the cerebellum (49%).
source: 24 of 49 in the cerebellum (49% - Figure 2G)
evidence: This is a result from comparing cerebellum data from Datasets A and C using the same pipeline.

claim: Twenty-five genes called as ASE in Dataset B are called as strain-specific by ISoLDE of which 20 are Class-1+2.
source: Twenty-five genes called as ASE in Dataset B are called as strain-specific by ISoLDE of which 20 are Class-1 +2 (Supplementary file 1g) compared with only one overlapping parent-of-origin called gene, suggesting they were miscalled as imprinted in the original study.
evidence: This is a result from comparing strain-specific calls with ASE calls in Dataset B.

claim: Among 311 known and novel candidate genes, 169 genes were in the 50-60% bias group and 95 genes in the 90-100% group.
source: Overall, among the 311 known and novel candidate genes for which bias data was available, we observed a bimodal distribution with 169 genes in the 50–60% bias group and 95 genes in the 90–100% group (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the bias distribution analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Two-thirds of known imprinted genes (77.3%) were in the 90-100% bias group.
source: Notably, two-thirds of known imprinted genes (77.3%) were in the 90–100% group while only 12.1% of novel candidates show this high expression bias.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the bias distribution analysis.

claim: Only 12.1% of novel candidates show 90-100% expression bias.
source: Notably, two-thirds of known imprinted genes (77.3%) were in the 90–100% group while only 12.1% of novel candidates show this high expression bias.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the bias distribution analysis.

claim: Most novel genes (73.1%) were found to have only weak biases with 50-60% expression coming from the preferred allele.
source: Most novel genes (73.1%) were found to have only weak biases with 50–60% expression coming from the preferred allele.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the bias distribution analysis.

claim: 88.7% of Class-1 novel singletons fall within the 50-60% weakly biased group.
source: 88.7% of Class-1 novel singletons and 83.9% of Class-2 genes in novel clusters fall within this weakly biased group (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the bias distribution analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: 83.9% of Class-2 genes in novel clusters fall within the 50-60% weakly biased group.
source: 88.7% of Class-1 novel singletons and 83.9% of Class-2 genes in novel clusters fall within this weakly biased group (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the bias distribution analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: 53.7% of Class-3 genes fall in the 50-60% bias group and 23.2% in the 90-100% group.
source: Interestingly, Class-3 genes, close to known imprinted regions, also show a bimodal distribution: 53.7% fall in the 50–60% group and 23.2% in the 90–100% group but, only nine genes (9.5%) show a 70–90% expression bias.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the bias distribution analysis.

claim: 70.3% of weakly biased Class-3 genes are preferentially expressed from the maternal chromosome.
source: Novel genes in known clusters (Class-3) follow the same trend of parental bias and direction (Figure 3B) with 70.3% of weakly biased genes preferentially expressed from the maternal chromosome and 64.5% of highly biased genes expressed from the paternally inherited chromosome.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis of bias direction shown in Figure 3B.

claim: 64.5% of highly biased Class-3 genes are expressed from the paternally inherited chromosome.
source: Novel genes in known clusters (Class-3) follow the same trend of parental bias and direction (Figure 3B) with 70.3% of weakly biased genes preferentially expressed from the maternal chromosome and 64.5% of highly biased genes expressed from the paternally inherited chromosome.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis of bias direction shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Weakly biased genes tend to be preferentially expressed from the chromosome with the methylated ICR (81% of Class-3 and 100% known <70% biased).
source: The direction of methylation does influence the bias as weakly biased genes tend to be preferentially expressed from the chromosome with the Meth-ICR (81% of Class-3 and 100% known <70% biased) whereas strongly biased genes tend to be preferentially expressed from the chromosome with the Un-ICR (80% of Class-3 and 54% known >70% biased -Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis of ICR methylation status shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Strongly biased genes tend to be preferentially expressed from the chromosome with the unmethylated ICR (80% of Class-3 and 54% known >70% biased).
source: The direction of methylation does influence the bias as weakly biased genes tend to be preferentially expressed from the chromosome with the Meth-ICR (81% of Class-3 and 100% known <70% biased) whereas strongly biased genes tend to be preferentially expressed from the chromosome with the Un-ICR (80% of Class-3 and 54% known >70% biased -Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis of ICR methylation status shown in Figure 3C.

claim: 83% of peripheral Class-3 genes (60/72) have a bias below the 70:30 canonical imprinting threshold.
source: Weakly biased novel genes are predominantly found at the periphery of annotated imprinted domains: 83% of peripheral Class-3 genes (60/72) have a bias below the 70:30 canonical imprinting threshold set by Andergassen et al., 2017 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis of gene position within clusters shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Only 13% (3/23) of novel genes flanked by known imprinted genes have a ratio below 70:30.
source: Conversely, highly biased Class-3 genes tend to be flanked by known imprinted genes: only 13% (3/23) of novel genes flanked by known imprinted genes have a ratio below 70:30 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis of gene position within clusters shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Fourteen highly biased Class-3 genes map between Ndn and Snrpn on chromosome 7.
source: Most of the 20 flanked, highly biased Class-3 genes belong to just two imprinted domains. Fourteen map between Ndn and Snrpn on chromosome 7 (Figure 4C) and five map downstream of Meg3 on chromosome 12 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a result from the genomic location analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Five highly biased Class-3 genes map downstream of Meg3 on chromosome 12.
source: Most of the 20 flanked, highly biased Class-3 genes belong to just two imprinted domains. Fourteen map between Ndn and Snrpn on chromosome 7 (Figure 4C) and five map downstream of Meg3 on chromosome 12 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a result from the genomic location analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Dync1h1 shows fully biallelic expression in E15.5 brain from maternal IG-DMR heterozygotes and wildtype littermates.
source: Dync1h1 which is located on the distal side of the region and was reported to be paternally biased in two of the original studies shows fully biallelic expression in E15.5 brain from maternal heterozygotes and wildtype littermates (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is an experimental result from the IG-DMR knockout validation experiment shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Wars and Wdr25 show a weak paternal expression bias in wildtype brains that is significantly reduced in mice with the IG-DMR deletion.
source: Conversely, two genes proximal to the defined cluster, Wars, and Wdr25, both show a weak paternal expression bias in wildtype brains that is significantly reduced in mice with the IG-DMR deletion (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is an experimental result from the IG-DMR knockout validation experiment shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The weak biases seen at the edges of imprinted clusters are regulated by the ICRs.
source: This indicates that the weak biases seen at the edges of imprinted clusters are regulated by the ICRs and may be innocent bystanders of the different epigenetic environments established by the ICR on each chromosome.
evidence: This is an inference based on the IG-DMR knockout experiment results.

claim: Of the eight novel singletons (Class-1) tested, four were biallelically expressed in all tissues.
source: Of the eight novel singletons (Class-1) tested, four were biallelically expressed in all tissues and indeed three were expressed at very low levels.
evidence: This is a result from the pyrosequencing validation experiments summarized in Table 1.

claim: Nhlrc1 showed a consistent paternal bias across all postnatal brain tissues.
source: One gene, Nhlrc1, showed a consistent paternal bias across all postnatal brain tissues (Table 1 and Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a result from the pyrosequencing validation experiments shown in Table 1 and Figure 5A.

claim: Nhlrc1 lies 1.3 kb downstream from a known germline DMR and a Zfp57 binding site.
source: It is noteworthy that this was the only Class-1 gene that was called in three of the original studies (Figure 1C and Supplementary file 1c). Nhlrc1 lies 1.3 kb downstream from a known germline DMR and a Zfp57 binding site suggesting a plausible mechanism for biased gene expression at the region (Proudhon et al., 2012; Strogantsev et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies identifying the DMR and Zfp57 binding site.

claim: In the P7 cerebellum, the Nhlrc1 DMR is partially retained with the maternal allele hypermethylated compared with the paternal allele.
source: In the cerebellum, the DMR is partially retained: the maternal allele is hypermethylated compared with the paternal allele in both BxC and CxB crosses (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a result from the bisulfite pyrosequencing experiment shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In the P7 liver, both alleles of the Nhlrc1 DMR are hypermethylated.
source: However, in the liver where Nhlrc1 shows no parental bias (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), both alleles are hypermethylated (Figure 5C), indicating Nhlrc1 expression is parentally biased only in tissues where the DMR is retained.
evidence: This is a result from the bisulfite pyrosequencing experiment shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Nhlrc1 expression is parentally biased only in tissues where the DMR is retained.
source: However, in the liver where Nhlrc1 shows no parental bias (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), both alleles are hypermethylated (Figure 5C), indicating Nhlrc1 expression is parentally biased only in tissues where the DMR is retained.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between DMR retention and expression bias.

claim: Of the 15 Class-2 genes tested, four fell below the expression threshold.
source: Four of the 15 Class-2 genes tested fell below the expression threshold (Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from the validation experiments summarized in Table 1.

claim: Of the 11 Class-2 genes with sufficient expression, six were biallelic in all tissues tested.
source: Of the other 11, six were biallelic in all tissues tested, two showed biased expression in the postnatal brain (Pcdhb12 and Wnk4) and three had a weak maternal bias in the placenta (Vat1, Rtn3, and Pla2g16) (Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from the validation experiments summarized in Table 1.

claim: Pcdhb12 shows preferential expression from the maternal allele in all postnatal tissues.
source: Pcdhb12 shows preferential expression from the maternal allele in all postnatal tissues which is consistent with the Datasets B and C (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a result from the validation experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Vat1, Rtn3, and Pla2g16 are three Class-2 genes that validated with maternal placental bias.
source: One of the other genes in the Wnk4 novel cluster, Vat1, was one of three Class-2 genes that validated with maternal expression bias in the placenta (Figure 5E). The other two genes Rtn3 and Pla2g16 form a novel cluster with Prdx5 (which is biallelic in all tissues tested) on Chromosome 19.
evidence: This is a result from the validation experiments shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Nine of the 20 Class-3 genes tested were validated in somatic tissues.
source: In contrast with the putative-biased genes identified elsewhere in the genome, we found those peripheral to known imprinted clusters were more likely to validate. Nine of the 20 tested genes were validated in somatic tissues (Adam23, Cox4i2, Bcl2l2, Tpx2, Smim17, Ifitm10, Wars, Wdr25, and Ago2 - Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from the validation experiments summarized in Table 1.

claim: Bcl2l1 and Ago2 showed a bias in all neural tissues tested.
source: Of these Bcl2l1 and Ago2 showed a bias in all neural tissues tested (Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a result from the validation experiments shown in Figure 6 supplements.

claim: Tpx2 was validated in all P60 tissues but not in the E16.5 or P7 material.
source: Interestingly, Tpx2 was validated in all P60 tissues but not in the E16.5 or P7 material (Table 1 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1) suggesting the bias strengthens over time postnatally.
evidence: This is a result from the validation experiments shown in Table 1 and Figure 6 supplement 1.

claim: Smim17 bias is strongest in the P7 hypothalamus (64.7%) but is reduced to 56.7% by P60.
source: Smim17 (Gm16532) is preferentially expressed from the maternal allele in five neural tissues (Figure 6—figure supplement 3). Smim17 bias is strongest in the P7 hypothalamus (64.7%) but is reduced to 56.7% by P60.
evidence: This is a result from the validation experiments shown in Figure 6 supplement 3.

claim: Wdr25 was biallelically expressed in all tissues except the P60 hypothalamus where 59.7% of expression is from the paternal allele.
source: Wdr25 was biallelically expressed in all tissues except the P60 hypothalamus where 59.7% of expression is from the paternal allele (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a result from the validation experiments shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Wars expression was consistently higher from the paternally inherited allele in all somatic tissues.
source: Unlike Wdr25, Wars expression was consistently higher from the paternally inherited allele in all somatic tissues however, the bias was only above the 55% cut-off in two tissues: e16.5 brain (55.1%) and P7 hypothalamus (56.2%) (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a result from the validation experiments shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Slc25a29 showed a very strong maternal bias in the placenta (81.1%).
source: Interestingly, Slc25a29 showed a very strong maternal bias in the placenta (81.1% - Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a result from the validation experiments shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Slc25a29 imprinting in the placenta is not under the control of the IG-DMR.
source: Allele-specific pyrosequencing revealed maternal and paternal heterozygotes to both the same degree of maternal bias as wildtype litter mates indicating that Slc25a29 imprinting in the placenta is not under the control of the IG-DMR (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is a result from the IG-DMR knockout validation experiment shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Canonical imprinting is defined as genes that are expressed predominantly (>70%) from one allele in a parent-of-origin specific manner in at least one tissue.
source: We, therefore, propose to define 'canonical imprinting' as genes that are expressed predominantly (>70%) from one allele in a parent-of-origin specific manner in at least one tissue.
evidence: This is a proposed definition by the authors based on their analysis.

claim: Canonical imprinted genes are under the control of a differentially methylated ICR that is established during gametogenesis.
source: Canonical imprinted genes are also under the control of a differentially methylated ICR that is established during gametogenesis with expression returning to biallelic levels or completely lost on perturbation of the ICR.
evidence: This is part of the proposed definition of canonical imprinting.

claim: Only two of the Class-1 or 2 genes tested validated in more than two tissues (Nhlrc1 and Pcdhb12).
source: Although many parental-origin-specific biased genes were identified in the brain in the original studies, only two of the Class-1 or 2 genes tested here were validated in more than two tissues (Nhlrc1 and Pcdhb12).
evidence: This is a summary of the validation results.

claim: The number of biological replicates can greatly influence the number of biased genes called.
source: Second, the number of biological replicates can greatly influence the number of biased genes called. We found that analysis of datasets with only one or two replicates (Datasets A and E) leads to a higher number of false positive novel biased genes being called compared with datasets with >6 replicates (Datasets B and C).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing results from datasets with different numbers of replicates.

claim: 22 of the genes experimentally tested had a strain bias in two or more tissues compared with 16 genes with parental origin bias in one or more tissues.
source: Moreover, 22 of the genes we experimentally tested had a strain bias in two or more tissues compared with 16 genes with parental origin bias in one or more tissues.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the validation experiments.

claim: The two Class-1 or 2 genes that experimentally validated in most tissues were both called by two or more of the original studies.
source: It is noteworthy that the two Class-1 or 2 genes that experimentally validated in most tissues were both called by two or more of the original studies suggesting a more accurate picture of ASE may be achieved by combining two calling methods.
evidence: This is an observation from the validation results.

claim: Only 6 of the 23 Class-1 and Class-2 genes validated experimentally (three in the placenta).
source: Although only 6 of the 23 we tested validated experimentally (three in the placenta) there may be others that display a true parent-of-origin bias.
evidence: This is a summary of the validation results.

claim: None of the Class-1 and 2 genes that were validated show a bias greater than 60:40.
source: None of the Class-1 and 2 genes that were validated show a bias greater than 60:40.
evidence: This is a summary of the validation results.

claim: There are three oocyte-methylated gDMRs in the novel cluster between Prdx5 and Pla2g16.
source: In the novel cluster between Prdx5 and Pla2g16 there are three oocyte-methylated gDMRs (Kobayashi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kobayashi et al., 2012.

claim: There are two oocyte-methylated gDMRs in the interval between Wnk4 and Rdm1, both of which overlap with Wnk4.
source: Interestingly, there are two oocyte-methylated gDMRs in the interval between Wnk4 and Rdm1, both of which overlap with Wnk4: one over the promoter and one over exons 5 and 6 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2; Kobayashi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kobayashi et al., 2012 and shown in Figure 5 supplement 2.

claim: The 22 Pcdhb isoforms exhibit allelic exclusion and are mono-allelically expressed in a stochastic and combinatorial fashion in individual neurons.
source: The 22 Pcdhb isoforms exhibit allelic exclusion and are mono-allelically expressed in a stochastic and combinatorial fashion in individual neurons so each cell expresses two genes from the maternally inherited chromosome and two from the paternal copy (Hirayama and Yagi, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hirayama and Yagi, 2017.

claim: Of the 60 tissue samples tested for Pcdhb12, 54 showed a maternal bias and only six showed a paternal bias.
source: This may reflect interindividual random bias: but, of the 60 tissue samples tested, 54 showed a maternal bias in Pcdhb12 and only six showed a paternal bias, indicating there are more neurons expressing the maternally inherited copy of the gene than randomly expected.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the validation experiments.

claim: Parental bias is stronger for known and novel genes within imprinted clusters than those at the periphery of the cluster.
source: We find that parental bias is stronger for known and novel genes within imprinted clusters than those at the periphery of the cluster.
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis of bias strength and gene position.

claim: Weak Class-3 genes are more likely to be repressed on the chromosome with the unmethylated ICR.
source: We have found that weak Class-3 genes are more likely to be repressed on the chromosome with the unmethylated ICR where repression of known imprinted genes relies on repressive histone marks.
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis of ICR methylation status and gene expression.

claim: Eight known imprinted regions have parental-origin-specific TADs in the postnatal cortex and hippocampus.
source: It has long been known that the Igf2/H19 cluster shows different conformation on each parental chromosome (Murrell et al., 2004) and a more recent single-cell 3D analysis found eight known imprinted regions have parental-origin-specific TADs in the postnatal cortex and hippocampus (Tan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Murrell et al., 2004 and Tan et al., 2021.

claim: Deletion of Bcl2l1 leads to loss of certain neuron types and reduction in brain mass upon paternal but not maternal transmission.

evidence: This is supported by a citation to Perez et al., 2015.
